In that case, which dealt with the Detroit, Mich., -Windsor, Ont., Canada, situation, the court held that the section 203(b)(8) exemption is applicable to the transportation of property between contiguous municipalities even though one such municipality is in a foreign country. The court's holding was based upon its view that the statute was clear and unambiguous on its face and should be given a literal interpretation in order best to fulfill its policy and intent. The court observed that the exemption was clearly directed to relieving this Commission of the burdensome and highly expensive tasks of regulating local cartage operations, and that application of the exemption to Windsor-Detroit traffic would not create a special problem of enforcement. Following the Verbeem case, it has generally been considered that local transportation between contiguous border municipalities is exempt from economic regulation under section 203(b)(8) and this Commission since that time has not asserted economic jurisdiction over local motor carrier operations between international boundary communities thought to be contiguous.
The Commission recognizes the apparent disparity this policy can create. Foreign carriers can operate within the exempt zone in the United States, but United States carriers cannot operate in foreign countries without a license because those countries have no rule comparable to our commercial zone regulations.
